questions.stem: Person perception refers to the:
options: process of explaining the causes of our own behaviour and that of other people
evaluation of an object, person or idea in terms of feelings, beliefs and actions
tendency to change our behaviour to match the behaviour of a group we belong to
mental processes used to form impressions and draw conclusions about other people
questions.explanation: Person perception is how we form impressions of others, often quickly and from cues such as appearance and body language. Explaining the causes of behaviour is attribution, which is related but is a separate process.

questions.stem: Within seconds of meeting her new teacher, Zara decides he is friendly because he smiles and makes eye contact. Zara's impression is mainly based on:
options: cognitive dissonance
the availability heuristic
non-verbal cues
an external attribution
questions.explanation: In person perception we use non-verbal cues such as facial expressions, eye contact and posture to form quick impressions. An external attribution explains behaviour by the situation, but Zara is judging what kind of person the teacher is.

questions.stem: An internal (dispositional) attribution explains a person's behaviour in terms of their:
options: personality, abilities, effort or other personal characteristics
situation, such as luck, task difficulty or the actions of others
membership of a social group with its own norms and roles
biological factors, such as the hormones released in the body
questions.explanation: Internal attributions locate the cause of behaviour within the person, such as their personality, ability or effort. Explanations based on luck, task difficulty or other people are external, or situational, attributions.

questions.stem: Mia says her friend failed the maths test because the questions were unfair and the room was too noisy. Mia has made:
options: an external attribution
an internal attribution
the fundamental attribution error
a self-serving bias
questions.explanation: Blaming the questions and the room explains the failure by the situation, which is an external attribution. The fundamental attribution error is the opposite tendency: overlooking the situation and blaming the person.

questions.stem: Which of the following situations shows the self-serving bias rather than the fundamental attribution error?
options: Reading only the news articles that support the views you already hold about a topic
Believing that most other people share your opinions more than they actually do
Blaming a poor mark on a noisy exam room but crediting a good mark to your own ability
Assuming a classmate failed because she is lazy, without considering that she was sick
questions.explanation: The self-serving bias is making internal attributions for our own successes and external attributions for our own failures, which protects self-esteem. Blaming a classmate's laziness without considering her illness is the fundamental attribution error, because it concerns someone else's behaviour.

questions.stem: In the tri-component model of attitudes, the affective component refers to:
options: the feelings or emotions a person has about the attitude object
the way a person acts or intends to act towards the attitude object
the beliefs or knowledge a person holds about the attitude object
the social group a person belongs to and shares the attitude with
questions.explanation: The tri-component model divides an attitude into affective (feelings), behavioural (actions) and cognitive (beliefs) components. The way a person acts towards the object is the behavioural component.

questions.stem: Which statement represents the affective component of an attitude towards snakes?
options: 'Many Australian snakes are venomous.'
'I always avoid walking in long grass.'
'Snakes should be kept away from homes.'
'I feel terrified whenever I see a snake.'
questions.explanation: The affective component is about emotion, such as fear. A statement that snakes are venomous is a belief, so it is cognitive, and avoiding long grass is an action, so it is behavioural.

questions.stem: In the 1930s, LaPiere travelled with a Chinese couple and they were refused service only once at many hotels and restaurants. Yet when later asked by letter, most of these businesses said they would not serve Chinese people. This illustrates that:
options: the behavioural component of an attitude does not always match the others
attitudes have only two components, as feelings and beliefs are the same
the cognitive component always determines how a person will behave
people's written answers are always a more accurate guide than actions
questions.explanation: The businesses' stated attitudes were not consistent with how they actually behaved, which is a key limitation of the tri-component model. If beliefs always determined behaviour, the businesses would have refused service, so the cognitive component does not always predict actions.

questions.stem: A stereotype is best defined as:
options: unfair treatment of a person because of their group membership
a mental shortcut used to judge how likely an event is to occur
a generalised, oversimplified belief about the members of a group
a negative feeling held towards a person because of the group they belong to
questions.explanation: A stereotype is a belief that members of a group share certain characteristics, which may be positive or negative. A negative feeling towards a group is prejudice, and unfair treatment is discrimination.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a positive role of stereotypes in social cognition?
options: They allow quick judgements by reducing the amount of information to process
They give accurate information about the characteristics of every individual
They prevent people from developing prejudice towards other social groups
They make people pay closer attention to each person's unique qualities
questions.explanation: Stereotypes are a form of mental shortcut that saves cognitive effort when we process information about the social world. Their cost is that they ignore individual differences, so they are often inaccurate about any particular person.

questions.stem: Cognitive dissonance is:
options: a mental shortcut that allows quick decisions to be made with little effort
the process of forming a first impression of a person from their appearance
the discomfort felt when a person's attitudes and behaviour are inconsistent
the tendency to explain other people's behaviour in terms of their personality
questions.explanation: Festinger proposed that people feel uncomfortable tension when their beliefs and actions conflict, and are motivated to reduce it. Explaining others' behaviour by their personality is an internal attribution, which is unrelated.

questions.stem: Jess believes vaping is harmful but continues to vape. To feel better, she tells herself that 'it's much safer than smoking cigarettes'. How is Jess reducing her cognitive dissonance?
options: by showing anti-conformity towards her peer group
by adding a new belief that justifies her behaviour
by changing her behaviour to match her attitude
by making an external attribution for her friends' vaping
questions.explanation: Jess keeps both her behaviour and her original belief, but adds a justifying cognition that makes the inconsistency feel smaller. Changing her behaviour would mean quitting, which she has not done.

questions.stem: A football fan believes his team's captain is honest. When reports of match-fixing appear, he dismisses them and reads only articles praising the captain. Which cognitive bias is helping him avoid dissonance?
options: false-consensus bias
hindsight bias
optimism bias
confirmation bias
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is seeking out and favouring information that supports existing beliefs while ignoring information that contradicts them. Hindsight bias is believing after an event that you knew all along it would happen, which is not what the fan is doing.

questions.stem: A student who copies parts of his assignments from the internet tells himself that 'everyone does it'. This belief, which helps him avoid dissonance, is an example of:
options: optimism bias
the fundamental attribution error
false-consensus bias
confirmation bias
questions.explanation: False-consensus bias is overestimating how many other people share our beliefs and behaviours, which makes our own behaviour seem more acceptable. Confirmation bias would involve selectively seeking supporting information, not assuming others behave the same way.

questions.stem: After her team loses the grand final, Priya tells everyone she 'knew all along' they would lose, although before the game she had predicted a win. This is an example of:
options: optimism bias
hindsight bias
anchoring bias
false-consensus bias
questions.explanation: Hindsight bias is the tendency, after an event, to believe the outcome was predictable all along. Optimism bias is about expecting good things to happen to us, which is closer to what Priya felt before the game than after it.

questions.stem: Many smokers believe they are less likely than other smokers to develop lung cancer. How does this belief help them avoid cognitive dissonance?
options: Optimism bias lets them keep smoking while believing they are not at risk
Anchoring bias makes them rely on the first health warning they received
Hindsight bias makes them think they always knew smoking was harmful
Attentional bias makes them focus more on health warnings about smoking
questions.explanation: Optimism bias is the belief that we are less likely than others to experience negative events, which reduces the conflict between knowing smoking is harmful and continuing to smoke. Focusing more on health warnings would increase dissonance rather than reduce it.

questions.stem: In decision-making, a heuristic is:
options: an explanation of behaviour based on a person's personality
a mental shortcut that allows quick decisions with little effort
a step-by-step procedure that always guarantees a correct solution
the discomfort felt when beliefs and behaviour are inconsistent
questions.explanation: Heuristics are rules of thumb that let us make judgements quickly, though not always accurately. A step-by-step procedure that guarantees a solution is an algorithm.

questions.stem: After seeing several news reports about shark attacks, Leah believes a shark attack at her local beach is much more likely than it really is. Leah is using the:
options: representativeness heuristic
affect heuristic
anchoring heuristic
availability heuristic
questions.explanation: The availability heuristic judges how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind, and recent, vivid news reports are easy to recall. The representativeness heuristic judges by how closely something matches a typical example, which is not the basis of Leah's estimate.

questions.stem: Tim is described as quiet, tidy and a keen reader. Asked if he is more likely to be a librarian or a salesperson, most people say librarian, though there are far more salespeople. This error comes from the:
options: affect heuristic
fundamental attribution error
representativeness heuristic
availability heuristic
questions.explanation: The representativeness heuristic judges likelihood by how closely someone matches a prototype, here a stereotyped librarian, while ignoring how common each group is. The availability heuristic depends on how easily examples come to mind, not on matching a description to a type.

questions.stem: Ellie buys a phone because the advertisement made her feel happy and excited, without comparing its features with other phones. Ellie has used the:
options: affect heuristic
availability heuristic
representativeness heuristic
anchoring heuristic
questions.explanation: The affect heuristic is making a decision based on current emotions rather than a careful weighing of information. The availability heuristic involves estimating likelihood from examples that come to mind, which is not what drove Ellie's choice.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the influence of heuristics on decision-making and problem-solving?
options: They always lead to correct decisions because they draw on experience
They are slower than step-by-step methods but are far more accurate
They are only used when a person has unlimited time to make a choice
They allow fast, efficient decisions but can lead to systematic errors
questions.explanation: Heuristics save time and mental effort, which is useful when decisions must be made quickly, but they can produce predictable errors and biased judgements. Step-by-step algorithms, not heuristics, are slower and more reliable.

questions.stem: What is the difference between prejudice and discrimination?
options: Prejudice is unfair behaviour; discrimination is a negative attitude
Prejudice is held by individuals; discrimination is held by groups
Prejudice is always unlawful; discrimination is sometimes lawful
Prejudice is a negative attitude; discrimination is unfair behaviour
questions.explanation: Prejudice is a negative attitude towards people because of their group membership, while discrimination is acting on such views by treating people unfairly. A person can hold prejudice without discriminating, which is why the two are distinguished.

questions.stem: A workplace requires all staff to work every Saturday. The rule applies to everyone but disadvantages employees whose religion does not allow work on Saturdays. This is an example of:
options: a positive stereotype about workers
indirect discrimination
direct discrimination
prejudice
questions.explanation: Indirect discrimination occurs when a rule that treats everyone the same unfairly disadvantages a particular group. Direct discrimination would involve treating someone less favourably openly because of their religion, which the rule does not do.

questions.stem: Having absorbed negative public attitudes, Elise has come to believe she is weak and to blame for her depression, so she avoids seeking help. This is an example of:
options: direct discrimination
a self-serving bias
self-stigma
public stigma
questions.explanation: Self-stigma is when a person internalises negative attitudes about a characteristic they have, such as a mental illness, and applies them to themselves. Public stigma refers to the negative attitudes held by others in society, which Elise has taken on.

questions.stem: Which is a likely effect on mental wellbeing of experiencing ongoing discrimination?
options: a lower risk of depression and loneliness
increased stress and anxiety, and lower self-esteem
greater trust in the people and institutions around them
a stronger sense of belonging in society
questions.explanation: Ongoing discrimination is a source of stress that is linked to anxiety, depression and lower self-esteem. It tends to reduce trust and a sense of belonging rather than increase them.

questions.stem: According to the contact hypothesis, which conditions are most likely to reduce prejudice between two groups?
options: brief contact in which one group has more power than the other group
competition between the groups for a prize that only one can win
keeping the groups apart so there is no opportunity for conflict
sustained contact between groups of equal status with a shared goal
questions.explanation: Contact reduces prejudice when it is sustained, the groups have equal status, they cooperate towards a common goal and the contact is supported by authorities. Competition for a prize only one group can win tends to increase hostility.

questions.stem: In Sherif's Robbers Cave study, hostility developed between two groups of boys at a summer camp. Which approach reduced the hostility most effectively?
options: bringing the groups together for shared meals and movie nights
holding more sporting contests between the two rival groups
keeping the groups separate for the remainder of the camp
setting superordinate goals that needed both groups to cooperate
questions.explanation: Hostility fell when the boys had to work together on goals neither group could achieve alone, such as fixing the water supply. Simply bringing the groups together for meals actually led to more conflict, showing that contact alone is not enough.

questions.stem: Players obey their coach's instructions because they fear being dropped from the team if they do not. Which type of power is the coach mainly using?
options: referent power
coercive power
reward power
expert power
questions.explanation: Coercive power is based on the ability to punish or impose negative consequences. Reward power works in the opposite way, through the ability to give something people want.

questions.stem: In the Stanford Prison Experiment, university students randomly assigned as guards became increasingly harsh towards the 'prisoners'. The study is mainly used to illustrate:
options: the influence of social roles and situations on individual behaviour
the influence of personality traits on who chooses to become a guard
the ability of individuals to resist pressure from those in authority
the role of the cerebellum in controlling aggressive behaviour
questions.explanation: Because the roles were assigned randomly, the change in behaviour was attributed to the situation and the roles rather than to the students' personalities. The study was stopped after six days, earlier than planned, and has been widely criticised on ethical grounds.

questions.stem: Compared with people from individualist cultures, people from collectivist cultures are generally more likely to:
options: value independence and personal achievement above all else
resist conforming to the group's norms in public settings
make internal attributions for most of the behaviour they see
put the goals and harmony of the group ahead of personal goals
questions.explanation: Collectivist cultures emphasise interdependence and group harmony, and studies have found higher levels of conformity in them. Valuing independence and personal achievement is characteristic of individualist cultures.

questions.stem: What is the difference between obedience and conformity?
options: Obedience happens only in experiments; conformity happens in everyday social situations
Obedience is always harmful to the individual; conformity is always helpful to them
Obedience follows a direct instruction from an authority; conformity follows group norms
Obedience follows group norms; conformity follows a direct instruction from an authority
questions.explanation: Obedience is doing what an authority figure tells you to do, while conformity is adjusting your behaviour to match a group, usually without being directly told. Both occur in everyday life, and either can be helpful or harmful.

questions.stem: In Milgram's original obedience study, about what percentage of participants continued to give shocks up to the maximum of 450 volts?
questions.explanation: Twenty-six of the 40 participants, about 65%, obeyed to the end, far more than experts had predicted. The finding showed how powerfully a legitimate authority figure can influence behaviour.

questions.stem: In one variation of Milgram's study, the experimenter gave instructions by telephone from another room, and obedience fell sharply. This shows the influence of:
options: group pressure from other teachers in the room
the personality of the individual participants
the social proximity of the authority figure
the legitimacy of the location of the study
questions.explanation: When the authority figure is physically distant, people feel less pressure to obey. The location was the same in this variation and no other teachers were present, so neither legitimacy of location nor group pressure explains the fall.

questions.stem: Milgram's procedures are widely criticised on ethical grounds. Which criticism is accurate?
options: Participants were children, so informed consent could not legally be obtained
Participants were forced to take part, so their participation was not voluntary
The experimenter's prods made it hard for participants to use their right to withdraw
Participants' names and results were published, breaching their confidentiality
questions.explanation: When participants hesitated, the experimenter used prods such as 'you have no other choice, you must go on', which undermined their right to withdraw. The participants were adult volunteers recruited by advertisement, so the other criticisms are factually wrong.

questions.stem: In Asch's line-judgement studies, conformity dropped sharply when one confederate gave the correct answer. This shows the importance of:
options: the size of the group
informational influence
deindividuation
unanimity of the group
questions.explanation: When the group is not unanimous, a single dissenter gives the participant support to resist, so conformity falls. Group size did not change in this variation; only the unanimity of the majority was broken.

questions.stem: Which finding about group size did Asch report?
options: Conformity rose as the majority grew to a few people, then levelled off
Conformity rose steadily with every extra confederate that was added
Conformity was highest when only one confederate was present
Group size had no effect on conformity at any size of majority
questions.explanation: Asch found that conformity increased as the majority grew from one to about three confederates, but adding more beyond that made little further difference. The belief that each extra person keeps increasing conformity is a common misreading of his findings.

questions.stem: On her first day in a new job, Liz copies her colleagues' way of filling in forms because she is unsure of the correct procedure. Later, she laughs at her manager's jokes so that the team will like her. Which describes these two behaviours, in order?
options: obedience, then informational influence
normative influence, then obedience
informational influence, then normative influence
normative influence, then informational influence
questions.explanation: Conforming because others are seen as a source of correct information is informational influence, while conforming in order to be liked and accepted is normative influence. Nobody gave Liz an instruction, so neither behaviour is obedience.

questions.stem: In a large crowd at night, some fans wearing masks damage property in ways they would never do alone. Which factor best explains this?
options: informational influence
reward power
deindividuation
social loafing
questions.explanation: Deindividuation is the loss of a sense of individual identity and responsibility in a group, especially when anonymous, which can lead to behaviour a person would not show alone. Social loafing is putting in less effort on a group task, which is a different effect.

questions.stem: In a group assignment where only the final product is marked, Josh puts in much less effort than he would if working alone. This is an example of:
options: anti-conformity
normative influence
social loafing
deindividuation
questions.explanation: Social loafing is the tendency to put in less effort when working in a group, especially when individual contributions cannot be identified. Deindividuation involves losing a sense of personal identity, usually in a crowd, rather than simply reducing effort.

questions.stem: After scrolling through friends' edited holiday photos, Ella feels that her own life is dull and her mood drops. This is an example of:
options: downward social comparison
the availability heuristic
informational influence
upward social comparison
questions.explanation: Upward social comparison is comparing ourselves with people we see as better off, which can lower mood and self-esteem, especially when images are idealised. Downward social comparison is comparing with people seen as worse off, which tends to make people feel better.

questions.stem: Social media apps deliver likes and notifications at unpredictable times. Why can this encourage addictive checking behaviour?
options: Predictable rewards are more satisfying, so users check to find them
Notifications reduce the brain's response to rewards, causing boredom
Users conform to the app's instructions out of obedience to authority
Unpredictable rewards keep people checking in case a reward has arrived
questions.explanation: Rewards that arrive unpredictably keep a behaviour going strongly, because any check might be rewarded. Predictable rewards are easier to stop seeking, so they are less likely to produce compulsive checking.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a positive influence of social media on wellbeing?
options: being exposed to misinformation that spreads quickly online
staying connected with distant friends and joining support groups
comparing oneself with edited and filtered images of other people's lives
losing sleep because of late-night scrolling and notifications
questions.explanation: Social media can strengthen social connections and give access to support communities, which can benefit wellbeing. Comparing ourselves with edited images is linked to lower mood and self-esteem.

questions.stem: Algorithms show users more of the content they already engage with, so people see mostly views that match their own. How might this affect group behaviour?
options: It makes users less likely to conform to the views of their group
It prevents misinformation from spreading between different groups
It can strengthen existing views and increase division between groups
It exposes users to a balanced range of views, reducing disagreement
questions.explanation: Seeing mainly agreeing views can create echo chambers that reinforce what people already believe and increase polarisation. Because these feeds narrow rather than broaden the views people see, they do not give users a balanced range.

questions.stem: Kate always does the opposite of what her friends do, deliberately wearing whatever is unfashionable. In psychology, her behaviour is best described as:
options: deindividuation
social loafing
anti-conformity
independence
questions.explanation: Anti-conformity is deliberately going against a group's norms, so the behaviour is still shaped by the group. Independence means making a choice on its own merits regardless of the group's view, which would not lead Kate to reject every trend automatically.

questions.stem: A committee is about to agree on a risky plan without discussing alternatives. Which strategy is most likely to empower members to make an independent decision?
options: having the leader announce their preferred option at the start
requiring members to show agreement publicly by raising hands
shortening the discussion so the decision can be made quickly
asking one member to argue against the plan and inviting dissent
questions.explanation: Encouraging dissent breaks the group's unanimity, which reduces conformity pressure and helps members voice their own views. A leader announcing a preference first and public voting both increase pressure to go along with the group.
